title: Acute pulmonary oedema
status: draft - clinically reviewed by project lead 2026-11-18; doses pending JRCALC check
dispatch: 03:40. 78-year-old female, difficulty in breathing, woke from sleep. Conscious and breathing. Called by husband.

sounds._note: Empty = subtitle/visual only. External = through the air near the face; chest = stethoscope (later versions).

breathing_external._note: Inverse-square fall-off: full volume within ~0.45 m, about -12 dB at 0.9 m, -24 dB at 1.8 m, barely audible across the room.

behaviour.notes: Knows the conditions but not doses; hands over the medicines box. Vague on timings until asked twice. Downplays the ankles until asked if they are worse.

props.description: Three pillows stacked at one end of the sofa
Plastic tub of medicine packets. The furosemide packet is still sealed, dispensed two weeks ago.

past_medical: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (2023)
history.medications_todo: Doses deliberately not shown in-app until checked against current JRCALC/BNF before release.
history.key_event: Stopped furosemide about 5 days ago because of night-time urination; ankles more swollen all week.
history.previous_episode: Admitted with pulmonary oedema last winter.

answers.text: Woke up... couldn't breathe... like drowning.
About three. She sat bolt upright and came down to the sofa, said she couldn't lie down.
Last winter... water on my lungs.
Tight... not pain. Just... can't get air.
Bit of a cough... frothy stuff.

questions.label: Any fever, or been unwell recently?

answers.text: No temperature. She's not had a cold or anything.
Her ankles are always a bit puffy.

questions.label: Are the ankles worse than usual?

answers.text: Well... yes, now you say it. Both of them, all week. She's not said they hurt.
On three pillows for about a week. She says she gets breathless lying flat.
Heart failure, blood pressure, an irregular heartbeat, diabetes, high cholesterol, and arthritis in her knees.
Oh, loads. The water tablet, the blood thinner, the heart ones... it's all in the box, here.
Stopped... water tablet... up all night.

questions.label: When exactly did she stop it?
When did you last eat or drink?

answers.text: Fish and chips for tea, about six.

questions.label: How far can you usually walk?

answers.text: To the shops and back, slowly. Not this week though.

first_impression.finding: Bolt upright on the edge of the sofa, tripod, frightened, won't lie back.
Fast (about 32 a minute if you count), shoulders lifting, neck muscles working.
3-4 words per breath, gasps between phrases.
Wet, bubbly breathing audible without a stethoscope; occasional cough.
Frothy, pink-tinged sputum on a tissue.
Pale and grey, sweaty forehead and upper lip.
Both ankles swollen; pressing leaves a dent; calves soft, not tender.
Neck veins visibly full while sitting upright.

later_versions.auscultation: Fine bibasal crackles to mid-zones bilaterally; scattered expiratory wheeze

debrief.opening_prompt: Before the explanation: say out loud what you think is going on and why.
debrief.doc: Scenario 01 - Acute pulmonary oedema (Claude doc, clinical source of truth for this file)

impression_options.label: Acute pulmonary oedema / acute heart failure

urgency_options.label: Urgent, but time to assess fully

answer.summary: acute pulmonary oedema (acute heart failure), brought on by stopping her furosemide five days ago. Time critical: severe work of breathing in a frail 78-year-old.

first_impression.intro: First impression, using the Patient Assessment Triangle (PAT): appearance, work of breathing and circulation to the skin.

items.why: Alert and talking means she is still compensating; drowsiness would mean she is tiring.
Pale, grey and sweaty points to a very unwell patient, before any observations.
Tripod and refusing to lie back: classic of severe breathlessness, and of fluid on the lungs (orthopnoea).
A rate around 32 with accessory muscles working is severe respiratory distress.
Only a few words per breath is a simple, powerful severity sign.
Wet, bubbly breathing you can hear from the doorway suggests fluid in the airways.
Frothy, pink-tinged sputum is a strong pointer to pulmonary oedema.
Cool, clammy hands: her circulation is under strain.
Fast and irregularly irregular: AF, which she has, and which can worsen heart failure.

nice_to_spot.why: Pitting ankle oedema fits fluid overload, and the calves being soft and non-tender makes a DVT/PE less likely.
Full neck veins while sitting up support raised pressure on the right side of the heart.

key.why: She stopped her furosemide five days ago: the likely trigger. The sealed packet in the medicines box shows it too.
Her medicines (furosemide, ramipril, bisoprolol, spironolactone, dapagliflozin) tell you she has heart failure even before she says so.
Known heart failure, AF, hypertension and diabetes: high risk for exactly this.
Admitted with the same thing last winter.
Woke at 3am and had to sit up: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, typical of heart failure.

supporting.why: Needing more pillows (orthopnoea) builds the picture.
Worse all week: fluid building up since stopping the tablets.
Penicillin allergy matters if a chest infection is being considered.

pertinent_negatives.why: Tightness but no actual pain makes a heart attack less likely as the cause, but not impossible: get a 12-lead ECG.
A cough with frothy sputum rather than green phlegm points away from infection.
No fever or recent illness makes a chest infection less likely.

scene.why: Reading the medicines box shows the sealed furosemide and her heart failure medicines.
Pillows stacked on the sofa: she can't lie flat. No need to check it, but it's there to notice.

differentials.name: Acute pulmonary oedema
differentials.for: Known heart failure, stopped furosemide, sudden breathlessness at night, can't lie flat, wet breathing, pink frothy sputum, ankle oedema.

differentials.name: Heart attack (MI / ACS)
differentials.for: Can cause pulmonary oedema, can be painless in older people and people with diabetes.
differentials.against: No chest pain. Get a 12-lead ECG: an MI can be the trigger.

differentials.name: Pulmonary embolism
differentials.against: On apixaban; lungs wet, not clear; calves soft and non-tender; bilateral ankle swelling.

differentials.name: Chest infection (LRTI)
differentials.against: No fever or recent illness; frothy pink sputum rather than green; a clear trigger (stopped furosemide).

differentials.name: COPD exacerbation
differentials.for: Breathless, tripod, some wheeze can occur in heart failure too.
differentials.against: No COPD history; wet crackly breathing and frothy sputum rather than mainly wheeze; a heart failure history and trigger.

next_steps: ABCDE: find and treat life-threatening problems first, then assess, form your impression and treat.
Oxygen for low saturations, to the target in JRCALC.
GTN, if her blood pressure and the JRCALC criteria allow.
Close to hospital: oxygen, GTN, pre-alert for her work of breathing, and go on blue lights.
Longer journey: as above, plus cannulate and give IV furosemide as per JRCALC.
Keep her sitting up; don't lie her flat.
debrief.coming_later: In later versions you'll measure her observations and listen to her chest. For reference, she would have: RR 32, SpO2 87% on air, HR 112 AF, BP 176/98, temp 36.8, GCS 15, BM 9.4, CRT 3 s; fine crackles at both bases up to the mid-zones, scattered wheeze; 12-lead ECG AF about 110, LVH, no ST elevation.
debrief.closing: This debrief reports what was available in the scenario and what was checked. It does not set what must be done: expectations vary between services and courses.
